As the Ferris wheel rotates with a constant angular velocity \( \omega \), the seats move past positions \( A \), \( B \), \( C \), and \( D \) as shown.

method.method_draft: Use an inertial-frame free-body diagram for the seat at position A. First read from the image that A is the top position of the Ferris wheel, so the center of the wheel is directly below the seat and the required centripetal acceleration points downward. From the text, use that the seat has mass m, is at radius R from the axis, and rotates with angular speed omega, so its centripetal acceleration is R omega^2. Take downward toward the center as positive. The forces in the radial direction are gravity mg downward and the axle force on the seat upward if it is supporting the seat. Apply Newton's second law radially: mg - F_axle = mR omega^2. Solve for the axle force: F_axle = mg - mR omega^2, upward. If the answer uses r instead of R, identify r as the same radius.

method.method_draft: Use the rotating-frame/apparent-weight viewpoint for the seat at A. From the image, note that A is at the very top of the wheel; the outward direction from the center there is upward, while gravity acts downward. From the text, read that the seat is fixed to the rotating wheel at radius R and angular speed omega. In the seat's instantaneous rotating frame, the seat is momentarily at rest, so introduce a centrifugal pseudo-force mR omega^2 directed outward, i.e. upward at A. Balance vertical forces in this non-inertial frame: upward axle force plus upward centrifugal force must balance downward weight, F_axle + mR omega^2 = mg. Therefore F_axle = mg - mR omega^2, upward, with r equivalent to the given R if the final expression uses r.
